subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Merton argued that the 'innovator' responds to strain by:
options: Accepting society's goals but using illegitimate means (e.g. crime) to reach them
Accepting both goals and legitimate means
questions.explain: The innovator accepts goals like wealth but turns to illegitimate means, such as crime, to achieve them.

questions.q: Durkheim, a functionalist, argued that a limited amount of crime can be:
options: Functional, e.g. reinforcing shared values and allowing social change
questions.explain: Durkheim argued some crime is inevitable and can be functional, reinforcing boundaries and enabling necessary change.

questions.q: 'Informal social control' includes:
options: Disapproving looks, ridicule or family pressure
questions.explain: Informal social control uses unofficial pressures like disapproval, gossip or peer pressure rather than official agencies.

questions.q: A 'victim survey' (such as the Crime Survey for England and Wales) is useful because it:
options: Can reveal crimes not reported to the police
Only counts crimes the police record
questions.explain: Victim surveys ask the public about their experiences, capturing crimes that never reached police records.

questions.q: Merton's 'strain theory' explains crime as resulting from:
options: A gap between society's goals (e.g. wealth) and the legitimate means to achieve them
questions.explain: Merton argued crime arises when people cannot reach culturally approved goals (like wealth) by legitimate means, creating strain.

questions.q: Feminist sociologists argue official statistics show women commit less recorded crime partly because:
options: Differential socialisation and informal controls make female offending less likely or less detected
Women are biologically incapable of crime
questions.explain: Feminists point to gendered socialisation and tighter social controls over women to help explain lower female crime rates.

questions.q: Reasons a victim might NOT report a crime to the police include:
options: That all crimes are automatically recorded
Believing the crime is too trivial or fearing they will not be believed
A legal duty to stay silent
questions.explain: Crimes go unreported for reasons such as seeming trivial, embarrassment, or distrust of the police.

questions.q: The process by which a labelled person commits more crime as a result of being labelled is called:
questions.explain: Deviance amplification describes how labelling and reaction can increase, rather than reduce, offending.

questions.q: Labelling theory, associated with Becker, argues that deviance is:
options: Created by society's reaction and the labels applied to certain acts and people
A fixed quality of an act
questions.explain: Becker argued no act is inherently deviant; deviance results from society labelling certain acts and people as deviant.

questions.q: Subcultural theories (e.g. Cohen) explain some crime as:
options: A response by some groups who form a subculture with alternative values
questions.explain: Cohen argued that some young people deprived of status form delinquent subcultures with alternative values.

questions.q: Durkheim argued that crime becomes 'dysfunctional' when:
options: There is a very small amount of it
There is too much (or too little) crime, threatening social order
questions.explain: For Durkheim, a limited amount of crime is functional, but too much can destabilise society.

questions.q: Self-report studies are a method of measuring crime in which:
options: People are asked anonymously about offences they have committed
questions.explain: Self-report studies ask people to reveal crimes they have committed, helping uncover unrecorded offending.

questions.q: 'White-collar crime' refers to crimes typically committed by:
options: Relatively powerful or professional people in the course of their work (e.g. fraud)
questions.explain: White-collar crime is committed by people of higher status in their occupations, such as fraud or embezzlement.

questions.q: Becker used the term 'master status' to describe how, once labelled, a person may be seen mainly as:
options: A 'criminal' or 'deviant', overriding their other identities
questions.explain: A master status means the deviant label dominates how others view the person, above all else.

questions.q: A common explanation for the link between social class and recorded crime is that:
options: Class has no effect on policing
Policing and the criminal justice system may focus more on poorer areas and groups
Only working-class people ever break the law
questions.explain: Recorded patterns may partly reflect that policing focuses on certain groups, while crimes of the powerful are less detected.

questions.q: Crime statistics consistently show that the group most likely to be convicted of crime is:
questions.explain: Recorded statistics show young males are the group most likely to be convicted of crime.

questions.q: A Marxist view of crime argues that:
options: There is no link between class and crime
Only the working class commit crime by nature
Crime is caused only by individual choice
The law and its enforcement serve the interests of the ruling class
questions.explain: Marxists argue the law is made and enforced in the interests of the powerful, while the crimes of the rich are often ignored.

questions.q: A 'folk devil' is best defined as:
options: A group portrayed by the media as a threat to society's values
questions.explain: Folk devils are groups demonised by the media as a threat, central to moral panics.

questions.q: Official crime statistics may be unreliable because:
options: Some crimes go unreported and recording practices vary
questions.explain: Official statistics under-record crime because not all crimes are reported or recorded consistently.

questions.q: What is the key difference between 'crime' and 'deviance'?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
Deviance is always more serious than crime
Crime breaks the law; deviance breaks norms but is not always illegal
questions.explain: Crime is behaviour that breaks the law, while deviance is behaviour that breaks social norms but may not be illegal.

questions.q: 'Formal social control' is carried out by agencies such as:
questions.explain: Formal social control is exercised by official agencies like the police, courts and prisons that enforce written rules.

questions.q: The idea of a 'moral panic', linked to the media, describes:
options: A calm public response to crime
An exaggerated public reaction to a group seen as a threat to society's values
questions.explain: A moral panic is an exaggerated, media-driven public reaction to a perceived threat, such as 'folk devils'.
